title: What will happen with the market?
author: baruhspinoza
selftext: Since making games is now getting easier and easier, what will happen with the market? I mean its saturated already, imagine if it will become 10x like this with AI.. Will it be possible to make money from games?

comments.author: vaksninus
comments.body: Better optioms for the consumer, good games will have an audience.

comments.author: hblok
comments.body:
Look at Amazon self-publishing. Before, there were 100 000 new titles uploaded every month. Now it's **300k every month**. 99.9% of that will go unnoticed, besides a handful of friends and family. It will be the same with games.

In fact, I bet the vast majority of games developed these days never get published. That's the case with my own collection. I've made some 20 games, but they're all for my son's handheld devices. I doubt they'll ever travel further than that. And that's completely okay.

comments.author: Practical-Elk-1579
comments.body: It will Probably end up into a spam folder if the quality remain that low.

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body: Discoverability will become worse, this will make gamers even more dependent on Steamers and Publishers.

replies.author: bledviolet
replies.body: Not really publishers anymore. They just push to streamers anyway lol.

replies.author: fsk
replies.body: Exactly this, more trash, harder discoverability.  Even though you can use AI to help you write a game, most of the ones I've seen so far are unplayable slop.  Since Steam still charges a $100 listing fee, that should keep the worst of the slop off Steam.

replies.author: baruhspinoza
replies.body: I think they should raise it to $300

replies.author: fsk
replies.body: One of the reasons Steam keeps it at $100 is fairness to non-US people.  On the other hand, the $100 listing fee hasn't been inflation-adjusted since it started.

replies.author: GigaTerra
replies.body:
It is too bad we can't use an tournament system, something like every week the games have to compete against each other, and the ones that win get to stay and the others have to go improve their game.

Because in an sense that is kind of what developers do for the listing fee, they publish their games on smaller stores, trying to earn money for the listing fee, but since it is just an fee some people are lucky and don't have to go to great lengths.

replies.author: Upset-Basil4459
replies.body: Word of mouth has always been the most important way of discovering games

comments.author: HippieYoHippieYay
comments.body:
All these ai games don't make any money. As always, only the very very few quality games will ever make any money at all.


Indie slop games BEFORE ai didn't make any money neither.

replies.author: MichaelEmouse
replies.body:
I saw a stat that 10% of games make any serious money which seems bad at first but there are so many low quality games that it isn't that bad. 

I'm curious if people will be able to make quality games while being assisted by AI though.

replies.author: dmelt253
replies.body: The thing with AI is it only amplifies the ideas of the end user. If 75% of the population is not creative or just has bad ideas then AI will only speed up the execution of bad ideas. But AI in the hands of someone with genuinely good ideas could be a game changer for that person. All we can do is shoot our shot and see what category we're actually in.

replies.author: Logical_Newspaper_52
replies.body: your stats are not even close to reality

replies.author: syn_krown
replies.body:
https://hub.synkrown.workers.dev

I have been programming for 20 years and now using AI when I need it, I think I am utilizing it correctly.

Check out my creations and you be the judge

replies.author: Noble_Nexus
replies.body:
Agreed, but just a simple correction "very very few popular games will ever make any money at all." 

It's not a matter o quality, it's a matter of popularity. There are some really good games out there with less than 1k players and some questionable shit with 50k plus because some streamer made fun of it in a video.

comments.author: benawheeler
comments.body:
Distribution becomes the moat, and yeah like you said since way more shitty games will likely come out, the bar will be higher to stand out. 

I think small game dev teams like 2-10 people will be the sweet spot. Polish goes a long way now that prototyping is so easy.

comments.author: ivyentre
comments.body:
Nothing changes.

AAA games still have the vastly superior funding and staffs, this the ability to outsell everyone.

replies.author: RyiahTelenna
replies.body:
>AAA games still have the vastly superior funding and staffs

Numbers? Yeah. Funding? Debatable. The main problem with AAA is that they don't actually want to fund most projects very well because it's risky. An indie studio that makes it big will typically apply those funds more generously. For example Hello Games.

comments.author: Primary_Dance9564
comments.body: thats acually a good question

comments.author: MURDERPALACE
comments.body: Ai game dev is practically content now. Much like music production and video.

comments.author: sharkymcstevenson2
comments.body:
There's alot of research on this subject, when supply gets bigger, demand actually gets bigger too - which doesnt make sense, but seems to be the case in most markets

I wouldn't worry too much! Great games will always win, bad ones won't

comments.author: bledviolet
comments.body: Shovelware didn't make money before AI, it won't make money after.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
it wasn't easy previously to begin with. 

it is similar to what happened to websites in the past e.g. making a simple HTML website used to be enough to get paid...

comments.author: StickStill9790
comments.body:
The Sony and Nintendo game stores are just buckets of trash with a few cherries on top. We’re gonna need a new “Nintendo Seal of Quality.”

People forget that was made because of the slew of terrible games once the Personal Computer became popular. Anyone could put together a couple of bits moving around. It was bad.

comments.author: monsterfurby
comments.body:
Making games is easy, but in a way, it has always been easy. Making good games though, is and always will be hard. Because it's not a formula. Even with GenAI, you still have to actually *design* the game, and you still have do the homework. Yeah, sure, coding becomes less technically, asset creation less expensive, but all that is worth bupkis if there's no creative vision behind the project, nothing remarkable on display.

So... yeah... shovelware will remain shovelware - it's just going to get even *more* annoying and omnipresent (kind of like the Greenlight/Xbox Arcade/early Nintendo eShop days), but there also might be an opening for more devs who otherwise would never have come that far to actually present some truly good games. It's gonna be one gem to a thousand turds, of course.

comments.author: benk09123
comments.body: Market was always saturated. Quality over quantity, thats what the stores are built around

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
We went through something similar in the 80's.

But if you can use AI to make a decent game cheaply, you might be able to make enough money to make another game cheaply.  As so on.  Until you create that 1 in a million.  

Another analogy.  Streamers.  Youtubers.  There are a lot of them.  Only a few are the super famous ones.  But there are plenty doing good enough to survive.  And more fail.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Slop didn't make money before. Won't make money now. Nothing changes.

It's still a long and difficult process to make an actual quality game. It may be easier, but it's not easy by any stretch. The only projects I've seen on here from people posting that are of any interest are usually in-progress shots of games that have had 6+ months in development and are still a long ways off from their intended release. Otherwise it's just half-assed clones of X genre-staple only worse in every way.

comments.author: dobkeratops
comments.body: hypersaturation . AI = creating for an audience of one.

comments.author: DegTrader
comments.body: At this rate, the Steam Store is going to need a 'Select AI-Generated Slop' filter just to find the actual games.

comments.author: MongooseEmpty4801
comments.body: Won't affect much. Yes it's easier, but it will just flood the market with more poor quality games, which 90% already are.

comments.author: MDRAR
comments.body:
It's simply become much easier to go from bad idea to publication. Good ideas are what sell. Bonus for the every-person is that we have more ability to execute good ideas than we did before.

Doesn't make having a good idea easier. Sadly modern tools do a poor job of helping people recognise what a good vs bad idea is 😄

comments.author: NocturnalReflections
comments.body: The cream rises to the top. With more and more games being released at higher and higher prices as the government prints more money devaluing your dollar more and more people will only by the best of the best or emulate the best of the best. You can still make money by building a game with AI but only if you make something truly fun and or truly good.

comments.author: Noble_Nexus
comments.body: We will need better curators and tags. Most asset flips games are really boring or poorly made. That don't sell. A studio that make this kind of lazy content will close doors faster than Ubisoft do something stupid, and they are the fastest stupids in the west.

comments.author: Own-Rub-2091
comments.body: I can't speak for everyone but it makes me feel like paying more than $40 for a game is crazy. These days I'm much happier supporting a independent developer (ai or not) rather than a multi billion dollar corporation.

comments.author: BillBangkok
comments.body:
Give me a good example of an AI game that sold well, please.

For me, AI is just a tool, as many have said here, but it will never help you create good game design. That requires 10,000 hours of experience for a game maker.

There are just tools that can help AAA or indie game makers, maybe to prototype or polish to their desired level, but the capability and skill are human behind the AI. And a lot of them require more experience or taste than you think.

What AI helps speed up the most, I think, is that it encourages more people to try creating games as a hobby. Maybe their goal is to put them live for people to play or maybe try to sell them, as I think many, including myself, once dreamed of being a game maker, and that's it.

But all quality is still the human behind the AI. If they slop, it's slop; if they craft, it's gold.

comments.author: poponis
comments.body: Making clone games and boring games is getting easier. People act that just because i have a hammer, I will make furniture and every body will buy them.

comments.author: FunMotionLabs
comments.body: My guess is the amount of content explodes, but attention doesn't. So the challenge shifts from making things to making things people genuinely remember, talk about, and come back to.

comments.author: YazzinDev
comments.body:
Making Games is not the hard part, but deciding what game to make and what to do and what to avoid. It will still be possible, but you won‘t get paid for just agreeing everything your AI tells you. 

This is the difference between ai slop and a modern game these days. I‘m currently also in the making of an game app which I‘m publishing soon, and realized that what matters is direction and human thinking, not the final code.

comments.author: DarkJayson
comments.body:
Look at youtube and videos, every minute over 500 hours of video is uploaded to youtube yet people still make a living from it.

If your game is good enough and you introduce it to people in the right way it will get an audience regardless of the process in which it was made.
